opus-5.5.text:
So the way I think about it, concept erasure is about making it impossible for any downstream classifier, within some class, to recover a particular concept from a representation. You can't just delete the neurons that happen to correlate with gender or part of speech, because information in these networks is distributed, superposed, and spread across lots of directions. So the real question is: after you've transformed the representation, can anyone still extract that concept?

In our work on LEACE, which stands for LEAst-squares Concept Erasure, we made that precise for linear classifiers. We asked what condition guarantees that no linear classifier can do better than a constant predictor at recovering the concept. The answer turned out to be surprisingly clean: the class-conditional means of the representation must all be equal. If the average representation for one value of the concept is the same as for every other value, no linear probe can use that difference, because the difference isn't there. Equivalently, the cross-covariance between the representation and the concept label has to be zero.

Once you have that necessary and sufficient condition, the next question is how to satisfy it while doing as little damage as possible to everything else the network knows. That's where the least-squares part comes in. We derived a closed-form affine transformation that achieves linear guardedness while minimizing the expected squared distance between the original and edited representations. It's essentially an oblique projection: you whiten the data, project out the subspace spanned by the cross-covariance, and then un-whiten. The whitening matters because a naive orthogonal projection can remove more variance than needed or leave correlated information behind.

I want to be honest about the scope, though. Linear erasure is not the same as erasing the concept from the network in some absolute sense. A sufficiently powerful nonlinear probe might still find the information, and the network's later layers are themselves nonlinear. So "erased" always means relative to a family of adversaries. That said, linear erasure is surprisingly meaningful in practice, because a lot of what models actually use seems to be linearly accessible. When we applied it at every layer, which we called concept scrubbing, we could substantially reduce a model's ability to use, say, part-of-speech information, and the model's performance degraded in ways that told us it had really been relying on that information.

So for me erasure serves two purposes. It's a practical tool for things like fairness, removing a model's ability to use a protected attribute. And it's a scientific tool: it lets you do causal interventions. If you surgically remove a concept and see what breaks, you learn something real about what the model depends on, which is much stronger evidence than just showing a probe can find the information.

r001.rationale: Defines erasure as making the concept unrecoverable by a classifier, and specifies that no linear classifier can do better than a constant predictor.

r002.rationale: Explicitly notes that a sufficiently powerful nonlinear probe might still find the information.

r003.rationale: States that LEACE seeks a condition under which no linear classifier can recover the concept better than a constant predictor.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way we approach it is pretty operational. When we say we want to erase a concept, what we actually mean is we want to make it so that nothing downstream can recover that concept from the representation. So if you've got some feature like, say, gender in a sentence embedding, or part of speech, or whatever the concept is, the question is: can I train a classifier on top of these representations and predict that concept? And if the answer is no, then in a meaningful sense the concept has been erased.

Now, there are different levels of that. The weakest version is linear erasure, which is what we focus on with LEACE, the LEAst-squares Concept Erasure method. The guarantee there is that no linear classifier can do better than chance at predicting the concept from the edited representation. And it turns out you can get a really clean closed-form solution for that. You take the representation, and you project out the part of it that's correlated with the concept labels, and you do it in a way that's provably the smallest change you can make, in a least-squares sense, while still getting that guarantee. So it's not just "some projection that works," it's the minimal one, which matters because you don't want to destroy everything else the model has learned in the process.

The reason I like the linear framing is that it's actually a surprisingly strong condition. If you think about it, saying no linear probe can pick up the concept is equivalent to saying the class-conditional means are all identical after erasure. And that's a very interpretable thing. It also connects to this broader picture in interpretability that a lot of concepts in these models are represented linearly, the linear representation hypothesis. So if that's true, linear erasure is kind of the natural unit of surgery.

Of course the stronger thing you might want is that no function at all, not just linear, can recover the concept. And that's much harder. In general you'd have to make the representation statistically independent of the concept, and that can require throwing away a huge amount of information. There are some nice theoretical results showing that for arbitrary nonlinear adversaries, you basically can't do much better than just destroying the representation. So I think of linear erasure as the sweet spot where you get a real guarantee, you can compute it cheaply, and you can even apply it at every layer of a transformer during the forward pass and see what the model does when it's forced to not use a certain concept.

And honestly that last part is the thing I find most interesting, because it turns erasure from a fairness or privacy tool into an interpretability tool. You erase part-of-speech information from every layer and see how much the language modeling loss goes up, and that tells you something about how much the model was actually relying on that concept, as opposed to just encoding it incidentally.

r001.rationale: It defines erasure operationally as making the concept unpredictable from the representation by a trained classifier, with chance-level prediction as the criterion.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes linear erasure from the stronger condition that no function can recover the concept, noting that the latter is harder.

r003.rationale: It says LEACE guarantees that no linear classifier can do better than chance at predicting the concept from the edited representation.

astra-6.text:
I think you first have to specify what it means for a concept to be represented. One way to operationalize that is through prediction: if I give you the network’s activations, can you predict whether the input has some property? If you can, then there’s information about that property in the representation.

Concept erasure asks whether we can transform those activations so that you can no longer make that prediction, while preserving as much of the other information as possible. And the important qualification is: what kind of predictor are we talking about? If you prevent a linear classifier from recovering the concept, that doesn’t necessarily mean a nonlinear classifier couldn’t recover it. You’ve erased it relative to a particular class of readouts.

So I wouldn’t interpret that as literally removing an idea from the network’s mind. It’s a precise intervention on a representation, with a guarantee about what information is accessible in a particular way. Whether that also stops the network from using the concept in its behavior is a further question.

r001.rationale: The response frames erasure as making the concept no longer predictable from activations, but does not specify a trained probe or the better-than-chance threshold.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says that blocking recovery by a linear classifier does not rule out recovery by a nonlinear classifier.

r003.rationale: It discusses preventing linear readouts from recovering a concept, but does not state that LEACE aims to do so.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to operationalize that relative to some class of ways of reading information out of the representation. Suppose you have a hidden state and a label for the concept you want to erase. You could ask: can a linear classifier predict that label from the hidden state? Then a fairly precise notion of erasure is to transform the representation so that no linear classifier can predict the label better than a classifier that only knows the base rates.

But that qualification—linear—is doing a lot of work. Information might still be accessible to a nonlinear classifier. If you demanded that no possible function could recover it, you'd be asking for statistical independence, which is a much stronger condition.

And there's another distinction between information being available and the network actually using it. Making a concept unreadable by a particular kind of probe doesn't automatically establish that you've removed every way it could influence the model's behavior. So I wouldn't think of it as finding the little object in the network corresponding to a concept and deleting it. It's more about specifying what information should become inaccessible, to which observers, while preserving as much of the rest of the representation as possible.

r001.rationale: It defines erasure as making the label no more predictable by a linear classifier than by a classifier using only base rates, an equivalent baseline for the criterion’s chance-level prediction target.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says information may remain accessible to a nonlinear classifier even when a linear probe cannot recover it.

r003.rationale: It states that the representation can be transformed so no linear classifier can predict the target label above the base-rate baseline, which conveys the stated linear-extraction goal.
